title: Inquest will be held in Toronto police fatally shooting mentally ill man who had pellet gun
subtitle: Two years after he was shot dead by Toronto police, the Ontario government announced Tuesday it will hold an inquest into the death of Ian Pryce.
article: Two years after he was shot dead by Toronto police during a standoff downtown, the Ontario government announced Tuesday it will hold an inquest into the death of Ian Pryce .
Long awaiting information about her son's final hours, Heather Thompson believes she may now get some closure.
"I have mixed feelings about this," Thompson said in an interview Tuesday, saying it's going to be difficult to listen to the details of her son's death.
"But I'm doing it so that I can move on."

Pryce, 30, was killed by two unnamed Toronto police officers on Nov. 13, 2013 near Sherbourne and Carlton Sts., after a standoff with the Toronto police Emergency Task Force . Thompson says her son had been living with schizophrenia for more than a decade.

According to the province's Special Investigation's Unit - the civilian watchdog that probes deaths involving police - Pryce was wielding a weapon that looked like a firearm, though police later discovered it was not real.
"In the aftermath of the incident, it was discovered that the man was actually armed with a pellet gun, not a genuine firearm," Tony Loparco, director of the SIU, said in a statement in January.

Loparco ruled there were no grounds to criminally charge either of officers involved in Pryce's death. The officers "acted in the reasonable belief that the lives of their team members and other officers were in imminent peril," he wrote.
When releasing Loparco's decision last year, the SIU did not identify Pryce by name, citing a policy that family consent is required to identify the victim of a fatal police shooting.

The Star independently confirmed Pryce's identity, and Thompson said she, in fact, wanted her son's name to be public in order to raise awareness about mental health issues and prevent another fatal police encounter. (Thompson said she asked the SIU not to release his name the same day she was told of his death. She would have consented to its release had she been asked when the watchdog completed its probe more than a year later.)
Ontario's ministry of community safety announced Tuesday an inquest would be held into Pryce's death - but did not specify when.

Under the province's Coroners Act, a death that occurs during a police detention warrants a mandatory inquest. However, some legal experts have argued that the question of whether someone was "detained" is open to interpretation and that there is no guarantee an inquest will occur when someone dies during an interaction or standoff with police.

Until last week, Thompson said she had been anxiously awaiting confirmation an inquest would occur. She hopes the information it uncovers will help prevent similar fatal encounters though she admits to being pessimistic.
"I don't think anything is going to change any time soon," Thompson said.

A few months before Pryce's death - prompted by the fatal shooting of teenager Sammy Yatim by a Toronto police officer in July 2013 - the Toronto force commissioned an extensive review of its use-of-force during encounters with people experiencing an emotional or mental-health crisis.

Earlier this year, Toronto police announced they have implemented many of the recommendations from that review, conducted by former Supreme Court of Canada judge Frank Iacobucci, including additional training for officers on how to de-escalate tense encounters.
The force has also implemented recommendations from a recent triple inquest into the deaths of three mentally ill people at the hands of Toronto police.
